text: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial. All these things happen to them by reason of their ignorance of what is good and evil.
plain: Expect difficult people today. They act that way because they do not know better.

text: Remember how long thou hast been putting off these things, and how often thou hast received an opportunity from the gods, and yet dost not use it.
plain: You have had chance after chance and let them go. Stop stalling.

text: Thou must now at last perceive of what universe thou art a part, and of what administrator of the universe thy existence is an efflux, and that a limit of time is fixed for thee, which if thou dost not use for clearing away the clouds from thy mind, it will go and thou wilt go, and it will never return.
plain: Your time has a limit. Use it to clear your head or it is gone for good.

text: Every man's life is sufficient. But thine is nearly finished, though thy soul reverences not itself, but places thy felicity in the souls of others.
plain: Your life is short and you are handing your happiness to other people. Respect yourself.

text: Through not observing what is in the mind of another a man has seldom been seen to be unhappy; but those who do not observe the movements of their own minds must of necessity be unhappy.
plain: Ignoring what others think is harmless. Ignoring your own mind will wreck you.

text: Since it is possible that thou mayest depart from life this very moment, regulate every act and thought accordingly.
plain: You could die today, so act like it matters.

text: Though thou shouldest be going to live three thousand years and as many times ten thousand years, still remember that no man loses any other life than this which he now lives, nor lives any other than this which he now loses.
plain: Even a long life is only ever lived one moment at a time.

text: Remember that all is opinion.
plain: Most of what hurts is how you judge it.

text: Of human life the time is a point, and the substance is in a flux, and the perception dull, and the composition of the whole body subject to putrefaction, and the soul a whirl, and fortune hard to divine, and fame a thing devoid of judgment.
plain: Life is brief, shaky and unpredictable, and fame is a bad judge.

text: And, to say all in a word, everything which belongs to the body is a stream, and what belongs to the soul is a dream and vapor, and life is a warfare and a stranger's sojourn, and after fame is oblivion.
plain: Life is a fight and a short visit, and fame ends in being forgotten.

text: What then is that which is able to conduct a man? One thing, and only one, philosophy.
plain: Only philosophy can guide you through a life like this.

text: We must make haste, then, not only because we are daily nearer to death, but also because the conception of things and the understanding of them cease first.
plain: Move now. Time runs out and so does your sharpness.

text: Hippocrates, after curing many diseases, himself fell sick and died. The Chaldaei foretold the deaths of many, and then fate caught them too.
plain: The healer got sick and the fortune tellers died too. Nobody is exempt.

text: Thou hast embarked, thou hast made the voyage, thou art come to shore; get out.
plain: You have lived your trip. When it ends, get off the boat without fuss.

text: Do not waste the remainder of thy life in thoughts about others, when thou dost not refer thy thoughts to some object of common utility.
plain: Stop spending your life wondering what other people are up to.

text: Be cheerful also, and seek not external help nor the tranquillity which others give. A man then must stand erect, not be kept erect by others.
plain: Do not lean on others for your calm. Hold yourself up.

text: Short then is the time which every man lives; and small the nook of the earth where he lives; and short too the longest posthumous fame, and even this only continued by a succession of poor human beings, who will very soon die, and who know not even themselves, much less him who died long ago.
plain: Your time is short, your corner is small, and even legacy fades fast.

text: Hasten then to the end which thou hast before thee, and, throwing away idle hopes, come to thy own aid, if thou carest at all for thyself, while it is in thy power.
plain: Drop the daydreams and help yourself while you still can.

text: Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, sea-shores, and mountains; and thou too art wont to desire such things very much. But this is altogether a mark of the most common sort of men, for it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself.
plain: You do not need a getaway. You can go inside your own head any time.

text: Constantly then give to thyself this retreat, and renew thyself; and let thy principles be brief and fundamental, which, as soon as thou shalt recur to them, will be sufficient to cleanse the soul completely, and to send thee back free from all discontent with the things to which thou returnest.
plain: Keep a few simple principles and return to them to reset.

text: The universe is transformation: life is opinion.
plain: Everything keeps changing, and how it feels depends on how you see it.

text: Death is such as generation is, a mystery of nature; composition out of the same elements, and a decomposition into the same; and altogether not a thing of which any man should be ashamed, for it is not contrary to [the nature of] a reasonable animal, and not contrary to the reason of our constitution.
plain: Death is as natural as birth. Nothing to be ashamed of or to dread.

text: Take away thy opinion, and then there is taken away the complaint, "I have been harmed." Take away the complaint, "I have been harmed," and the harm is taken away.
plain: Stop telling yourself you were hurt and half the hurt goes away.

text: That which does not make a man worse than he was, also does not make his life worse, nor does it harm him either from without or from within.
plain: If it does not make you a worse person, it has not really hurt you.

text: Do not have such an opinion of things as he has who does thee wrong, or such as he wishes thee to have, but look at them as they are in truth.
plain: Do not take on the story your enemy wants you to believe. See things as they are.

text: Hast thou reason? I have.--Why then dost not thou use it?
plain: You have a brain. Use it.

text: Many grains of frankincense on the same altar: one falls before, another falls after; but it makes no difference.
plain: Some go early, some late. In the end it comes to the same.

text: Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good.
plain: You are not here forever. Do right while you still can.

text: How much trouble he avoids who does not look to see what his neighbor says or does or thinks, but only to what he does himself, that it may be just and pure; or, as Agathon says, look not round at the depraved morals of others, but run straight along the line without deviating from it.
plain: Watch your own lane. Ignoring what everyone else is doing saves a lot of trouble.

text: What is praise, except indeed so far as it has a certain utility?
plain: Praise is only worth something if it is useful.

text: Neither worse then nor better is a thing made by being praised.
plain: Praise does not make a thing better and blame does not make it worse.

text: Everything harmonizes with me, which is harmonious to thee, O Universe. Nothing for me is too early nor too late, which is in due time for thee.
plain: Whatever timing life gives you is the right timing.

text: Does any one do wrong? It is to himself that he does the wrong.
plain: When someone wrongs you, the damage lands mostly on them.

text: In a word, thy life is short. Thou must turn to profit the present by the aid of reason and justice. Be sober in thy relaxation.
plain: Life is short. Use today well, and keep your rest in moderation.

text: Love the art, poor as it may be, which thou hast learned, and be content with it; and pass through the rest of life like one who has intrusted to the gods with his whole soul all that he has, making thyself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any man.
plain: Love your craft even if it is modest. Do not rule anyone and do not serve anyone.

text: And, to conclude the matter, what is even an eternal remembrance? A mere nothing.
plain: Even being remembered forever is worth nothing.

text: Everything is only for a day, both that which remembers and that which is remembered.
plain: The one who remembers and the one remembered both last a day.

text: Thou wilt soon die, and thou art not yet simple, nor free from perturbations, nor without suspicion of being hurt by external things, nor kindly disposed towards all; nor dost thou yet place wisdom only in acting justly.
plain: You will die soon and you are still not calm, still suspicious, still not living right. Get on it.

text: Time is like a river made up of the events which happen, and a violent stream; for as soon as a thing has been seen, it is carried away, and another comes in its place, and this will be carried away too.
plain: Time sweeps everything away, and what replaces it gets swept away too.

text: Everything which happens is as familiar and well known as the rose in spring and the fruit in summer; for such is disease, and death, and calumny, and treachery, and whatever else delights fools or vexes them.
plain: Bad things are as ordinary as the seasons. Do not act surprised.

text: To conclude, always observe how ephemeral and worthless human things are, and what was yesterday a little mucus, to-morrow will be a mummy or ashes.
plain: Everyone is here briefly. Keep that in view.

text: Pass then through this little space of time conformably to nature, and end thy journey in content, as an olive falls off when it is ripe, blessing nature who produced it, and thanking the tree on which it grew.
plain: Live your short time well and leave with thanks, like ripe fruit falling.

text: Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it.
plain: Be the rock. Let the waves break on you and calm down.

text: Unhappy am I because this has happened to me? Not so, but happy am I, though this has happened to me, because I continue free from pain, neither crushed by the present nor fearing the future.
plain: This happened and I am still fine, not crushed and not scared of what comes.

text: Remember too on every occasion which leads thee to vexation to apply this principle; not that this is a misfortune, but that to bear it nobly is good fortune.
plain: The bad thing is not bad luck. Handling it well is the good luck.

text: Do not then consider life a thing of any value.
plain: Do not hold life so tightly that you freeze.

text: In this infinity then what is the difference between him who lives three days and him who lives three generations?
plain: Against infinite time, short and long lives are about the same.

text: In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present,--I am rising to the work of a human being.
plain: When you do not want to get up, remember that you are getting up to do a human's work.

text: Why then am I dissatisfied if I am going to do the things for which I exist and for which I was brought into the world? Or have I been made for this, to lie in the bed-clothes and keep myself warm?
plain: You were not made to lie in bed warm and comfortable. Get up and do the thing.

text: So thou lovest not thyself, for if thou didst, thou wouldst love thy nature and her will.
plain: If you loved yourself you would do the work you were built for.

text: How easy it is to repel and to wipe away every impression which is troublesome or unsuitable, and immediately to be in all tranquillity.
plain: You can wipe a troubling thought away and be calm right now.

text: Show those qualities then which are altogether in thy power, sincerity, gravity, endurance of labor, aversion to pleasure, contentment with thy portion and with few things, benevolence, frankness, no love of superfluity, freedom from trifling, magnanimity.
plain: Stop pointing at your weak spots. Show the traits that are fully up to you.

text: Dost thou not see how many qualities thou art immediately able to exhibit, in which there is no excuse of natural incapacity and unfitness, and yet thou still remainest voluntarily below the mark?
plain: There are a lot of things you can do right now with no excuse. You stay below your level by choice.

text: About what am I now employing my own soul?
plain: Where is my mind going right now?

text: Such as are thy habitual thoughts, such also will be the character of thy mind; for the soul is dyed by the thoughts.
plain: Your habitual thoughts shape who you are.

text: To seek what is impossible is madness: and it is impossible that the bad should not do something of this kind.
plain: Expecting bad people not to act badly is madness.

text: Nothing happens to any man which he is not formed by nature to bear.
plain: Whatever you face, you can bear.

text: It is a shame then that ignorance and conceit should be stronger than wisdom.
plain: It is a shame when ignorance and conceit beat wisdom.

text: Things themselves touch not the soul, not in the least degree; nor have they admission to the soul, nor can they turn or move the soul: but the soul turns and moves itself alone, and whatever judgments it may think proper to make, such it makes for itself the things which present themselves to it.
plain: Events cannot move your mind. Only your own judgments do.

text: Often think of the rapidity with which things pass by and disappear, both the things which are and the things which are produced.
plain: Things vanish fast. Remember that often.

text: How then is he not a fool who is puffed up with such things or plagued about them and makes himself miserable?
plain: Being puffed up or tormented over passing things is foolish.

text: Does another do me wrong? Let him look to it.
plain: Someone wronged you? That is theirs to deal with.

text: Art thou angry with him whose armpits stink? art thou angry with him whose mouth smells foul? What good will this anger do thee?
plain: You cannot change how someone is. What does your anger fix?

text: Soon, very soon, thou wilt be ashes, or a skeleton, and either a name or not even a name; but name is sound and echo.
plain: You will soon be ashes and even your name is just an echo.

text: And the things which are much valued in life are empty and rotten and trifling, and [like] little dogs biting one another, and little children quarreling, laughing, and then straightway weeping.
plain: What most people chase is petty, like squabbling kids and snapping dogs.

text: But to have good repute amid such a world as this is an empty thing.
plain: Being well thought of in a world like this means little.

text: Thou canst pass thy life in an equable flow of happiness, if thou canst go by the right way, and think and act in the right way.
plain: Steady happiness comes from thinking and acting right.

text: If this is neither my own badness, nor an effect of my own badness, and the common weal is not injured, why am I troubled about it, and what is the harm to the common weal?
plain: If it is not my fault and hurts no one, why am I bothered?

text: Let it make no difference to thee whether thou art cold or warm, if thou art doing thy duty; and whether thou art drowsy or satisfied with sleep; and whether ill-spoken of or praised; and whether dying or doing something else.
plain: Do your job whether you are cold, tired, praised or blamed.

text: Look within. Let neither the peculiar quality of anything nor its value escape thee.
plain: Look inward and see things for what they really are.

text: The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like [the wrong-doer].
plain: The best revenge is not becoming like them.

text: When thou hast been compelled by circumstances to be disturbed in a manner, quickly return to thyself, and do not continue out of tune longer than the compulsion lasts; for thou wilt have more mastery over the harmony by continually recurring to it.
plain: When life knocks you off balance, return to yourself fast. Do it enough and it gets easy.

text: It would be just as if a man should fall in love with one of the sparrows which fly by, but it has already passed out of sight.
plain: Loving what passes is like falling for a bird already out of sight.

text: Suppose then that thou hast given up this worthless thing called fame, what remains that is worth valuing?
plain: Drop fame and ask what is actually worth wanting.

text: How strangely men act! They will not praise those who are living at the same time and living with themselves; but to be themselves praised by posterity, by those whom they have never seen nor ever will see, this they set much value on.
plain: People stay stingy with praise today but crave the praise of strangers who are not born yet.

text: If a thing is difficult to be accomplished by thyself, do not think that it is impossible for man: but if anything is possible for man and conformable to his nature, think that this can be attained by thyself too.
plain: Hard for you is not impossible. If a human can do it, you can.

text: If any man is able to convince me and show me that I do not think or act right, I will gladly change; for I seek the truth, by which no man was ever injured. But he is injured who abides in his error and ignorance.
plain: Show me I am wrong and I will change. Truth never hurt anyone, staying wrong does.

text: I do my duty: other things trouble me not; for they are either things without life, or things without reason, or things that have rambled and know not the way.
plain: Do the job. The rest is noise from things that cannot think.

text: What then if they grow angry, wilt thou be angry too? Wilt thou not go on with composure and number every letter?
plain: They get angry and you stay steady and keep working.

text: Teach them then, and show them without being angry.
plain: Teach people without anger.

text: It is a shame for the soul to be first to give way in this life, when thy body does not give way.
plain: Do not let your mind quit before your body does.

text: Take care that thou art not made into a Caesar, that thou art not dyed with this dye; for such things happen.
plain: Do not let power change who you are.

text: Short is life. There is only one fruit of this terrene life--a pious disposition and social acts.
plain: Life is short, and the one thing it yields is good character and good deeds.

text: How many pleasures have been enjoyed by robbers, patricides, tyrants.
plain: Pleasure proves nothing. Even awful people enjoy plenty.

text: He who has seen present things has seen all, both everything which has taken place from all eternity and everything which will be for time without end; for all things are of one kin and of one form.
plain: See today and you have seen it all. The same patterns repeat forever.

text: One thing here is worth a great deal, to pass thy life in truth and justice, with a benevolent disposition even to liars and unjust men.
plain: What counts is living in truth and fairness, even toward liars.

text: Be not dissatisfied then that thou must live only so many years and not more; for as thou art satisfied with the amount of substance which has been assigned to thee, so be content with the time.
plain: You accept your body weight. Accept your lifespan too.

text: He who loves fame considers another man's activity to be his own good; and he who loves pleasure, his own sensations; but he who has understanding considers his own acts to be his own good.
plain: Fame lives in other people's hands, pleasure in feelings. Wisdom lives in what you do.

text: It is in our power to have no opinion about a thing, and not to be disturbed in our soul; for things themselves have no natural power to form our judgments.
plain: You can choose not to judge an event, and then it cannot shake you.

text: That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee.
plain: What hurts the group hurts you too.

text: How many together with whom I came into the world are already gone out of it.
plain: So many people I started with are already gone.

text: Why then am I angry? Dost thou think that a false opinion has less power than the bile in the jaundiced or the poison in him who is bitten by a mad dog?
plain: A false belief can poison you like venom. Check it before you get angry.

text: What kind of people are those whom men wish to please, and for what objects, and by what kind of acts?
plain: Look at who you are trying to impress and why.

text: There is nothing new: all things are both familiar and short-lived.
plain: Nothing is new and nothing lasts.

text: I can have that opinion about anything which I ought to have. If I can, why am I disturbed?
plain: I choose my view of things. So why let it bother me?

text: To recover thy life is in thy power. Look at things again as thou didst use to look at them; for in this consists the recovery of thy life.
plain: You can get your life back by seeing things the way you used to.

text: It is thy duty then in the midst of such things to show good humor and not a proud air; to understand however that every man is worth just so much as the things are worth about which he busies himself.
plain: A man is worth what the things he busies himself with are worth. Pick well.

text: How many after being celebrated by fame have been given up to oblivion; and how many who have celebrated the fame of others have long been dead.
plain: The famous and their fans are both gone.

text: Be not ashamed to be helped; for it is thy business to do thy duty like a soldier in the assault on a town.
plain: Take help without shame. Soldiers do.

text: Let not future things disturb thee, for thou wilt come to them, if it shall be necessary, having with thee the same reason which now thou usest for present things.
plain: Do not fear the future. You will meet it with the same mind you have now.

text: Let there fall externally what will on the parts which can feel the effects of this fall. For those parts which have felt will complain, if they choose. But I, unless I think that what has happened is an evil, am not injured.
plain: Let the blow land. The only real harm is deciding it is a disaster.

text: Whatever any one does or says, I must be emerald and keep my color.
plain: No matter what anyone does, stay yourself.

text: The leading principle in itself wants nothing, unless it makes a want for itself; and therefore it is both free from perturbation and unimpeded, if it does not disturb and impede itself.
plain: Your mind wants nothing until you invent a want. Stop getting in your own way.

text: Is any man afraid of change? Why, what can take place without change?
plain: Afraid of change? Nothing happens without it.

text: How many a Chrysippus, how many a Socrates, how many an Epictetus has time already swallowed up!
plain: Time has swallowed up the greatest thinkers. It will take us.

text: Near is thy forgetfulness of all things; and near the forgetfulness of thee by all.
plain: You will forget everything soon and soon be forgotten.

text: It is peculiar to man to love even those who do wrong.
plain: Loving even those who wrong you is what makes you human.

text: When a man has done thee any wrong, immediately consider with what opinion about good or evil he has done wrong.
plain: When someone wrongs you, ask what they believed they were doing.
